newsitem.title: GERMANY: German public TV ad rights should go-report.
newsitem.headline: German public TV ad rights should go-report.

text.p: German public TV and radio channels should lose their right to advertise and in future focus their programming on public-interest issues, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition said on Tuesday.

While stopping short of demanding the abolition of fee-based public broadcasters, Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) called for their privileges to be "seriously examined" in the context of a rapidly changing media landscape.

A decade after their launch commercial channels now fulfil many of the functions of public television -- whose share of advertising fell in 1995 to 10 percent of the 6.3 billion mark ($4.1 billion) total TV advertising market.
But even that is too much for Kohl's government -- which is uneasy with a public broadcast media whose role is anchored in Germany's post-war constitution.

Initially set up to ensure equal and fair coverage of a broad range of issues effecting the population, the public networks have been criticised recently as bloated bureaucracies and tools of party functionaries who sit on their boards.

Martin Mayer, CDU representative on a parliamentary media inquiry, told reporters the proliferation of other electronic media -- like on-line services -- threw into doubt the right of public TV and radio stations to special licence fee funding.
"The privileges of public broadcasters in financing and frequencies should be seriously examined," Mayer said, presenting an interim inquiry report.
He also said that technical progress would enable more channels to be broadcast, meaning that rules governing the granting of licences had also become outdated.
The market for electronic media -- where the trend is towards diversity and away from concentration -- should be treated in future more like that for newspapers, Mayer added.

"If the market for electronic media comes to resemble the newspaper market, licence obligations will come into conflict with the German basic law and special controls against media concentration will become unnecessary," Mayer said.
Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens did not support the interim report's conclusions. Mayer accused them of putting state interests before freedom of speech.
